title: One can never start a computer experiment with too simple a system

fields.label: Label
fields.value: One can never start a computer experiment with too simple a system

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Computer experiments should study the simplest possible systems with the simplest possible procedures, because simple systems already show complex behavior, and the most common mistake is studying systems far more complicated than necessary.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: in my experience the single most common mistake in doing computer experiments is to look at systems that are vastly more complicated than is necessary.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 3, “The World of Simple Programs”; section “How the Discoveries in This Chapter Were Made” (from p. 108), p. 110. Scope: design of computer experiments

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch03-23: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.17

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: No observation can establish that one can never start too simply, because usefulness depends on the scientific objective. Retrospective project data would test a narrower efficiency hypothesis, not the stated prescription.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The recommendation could be reframed as comparing scientific yield per unit effort across experiments of different model complexity, but no threshold defines too simple or necessary. Such a proxy would not resolve the absolute methodological prescription as stated.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Simplest possible and vastly more complicated than necessary are undefined and task-relative.

The claim is primarily normative advice.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a methodological maxim drawn from Wolfram's experience, together with the assertion that simple systems already suffice for complex behavior. The second idea is tested by other claims in the batch; this claim itself gives no population of experiments, no coding of 'mistake,' and no result that would show the maxim is wrong. It is not a statement that existing data can settle.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The claim is advice about experimental design: start with the simplest system, because extra complication is usually unnecessary. 'Too simple,' 'the most common mistake,' and 'interesting behavior' are not tied to a measured error rate or a decision criterion.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A complicated system that reveals something a simple one misses can be classified as a case where the simple system was not yet understood.

'The most common mistake' is an author's judgment about practice, not a count defined over a specified population of experiments.
